title: Idealism and Liberal Institutionalism

cards.b:
International Relations (IR) theory starts with a simple question: why do states fight, and can they ever live in lasting peace?

Idealism says yes. It grew out of the horror of the First World War (1914-18), which killed about ten million soldiers. Its leaders believed war could be prevented by law, public opinion and a world organisation.

Its modern descendant is liberal institutionalism, also called neoliberal institutionalism. It says states can cooperate even in anarchy, if institutions make cooperation easier.

This is the opening topic of Paper II Section A. Examiners ask about the idealist-realist debate, Wilson and the League, E.H. Carr's critique, the democratic peace, and Keohane and Nye on interdependence. Tie each of these to a year and a book, and you will score well.

All liberal IR thought rests on a few shared beliefs.

  • Human nature is not fixed in conflict. People can reason and cooperate.
  • War is not natural. It comes from bad institutions, secret diplomacy and autocratic rulers, and it can be reduced.
  • Harmony of interests. Nations gain more from trade and peace than from conquest.
  • Law and organisation can tame anarchy. International law, arbitration and a standing body can replace the "law of the jungle".
  • Public opinion and democracy restrain war.

Realists reject nearly all of this. That clash is called the first great debate of IR, held in the 1930s and 1940s between idealists and realists.

Note the label. "Idealism" was a name given by critics, mostly by Carr. The idealists thought of themselves as practical reformers.

Immanuel Kant wrote Perpetual Peace: A Philosophical Sketch (1795). It is the oldest source of liberal IR theory.

Kant's three definitive articles

  1. The civil constitution of every state should be republican. Citizens, not kings, decide on war, so they will hesitate.
  2. The law of nations should rest on a federation of free states. This is not a world state but a league of peace.
  3. Cosmopolitan right is limited to universal hospitality. Strangers must not be treated as enemies.

Kant also argued that trade would slowly bind nations together. His thinking shapes the democratic peace thesis and the idea of a league of nations.

Other early liberals: Hugo Grotius (De Jure Belli ac Pacis, 1625) on international law, Jeremy Bentham on a code of international law, and Richard Cobden on free trade as the path to peace.

cards.h: Wilson, the Fourteen Points and the League
cards.b:
US President Woodrow Wilson is the face of idealism. On 8 January 1918 he announced the Fourteen Points: open diplomacy, freedom of the seas, free trade, arms reduction, fair settlement of colonial claims, self-determination, and a general association of nations.

The League of Nations was set up in 1920 with its seat at Geneva. Its Covenant was part of the Treaty of Versailles. Article 10 protected members' territorial integrity. Article 16 provided economic and military sanctions against an aggressor.

The League was built on collective security: an attack on one is an attack on all.

The League had real weaknesses.

  • The United States never joined. The Senate refused to ratify the Treaty of Versailles in 1919-20.
  • Unanimity rule. Council decisions needed everyone's consent.
  • No army. Sanctions depended on members' will.
  • Germany and the Soviet Union were outside at first. Germany joined in 1926 and left in 1933. The USSR joined in 1934 and was expelled in 1939.

Then came the tests.

  • Manchuria (1931). Japan seized it. The Lytton Commission condemned Japan, and Japan left the League in 1933.
  • Abyssinia (1935). Italy invaded Ethiopia. Sanctions were weak and oil was never banned.

Other signs of failure: the Rhineland (1936) and Munich (1938). The Kellogg-Briand Pact (1928) had outlawed war as a tool of policy, but it had no enforcement.

The League formally ended in 1946. Its lessons shaped the UN Charter.

E.H. Carr, a British historian and diplomat, wrote The Twenty Years' Crisis, 1919-1939 (1939). It is the founding text of modern realism and the main attack on idealism.

Carr's main points

  • Idealists were utopians. They mistook wishes for facts.
  • The "harmony of interests" is not real. It is an ideology of the satisfied powers who want to keep the status quo.
  • Power and morality both matter. Politics needs both utopia and reality.
  • Ideas of international "justice" often reflect the interest of the strong.

The Second World War seemed to prove Carr right. For three decades after it, realism dominated IR, led by Hans Morgenthau (Politics Among Nations, 1948).

Fair note: Carr did not reject morality. He said pure realism, like pure idealism, is sterile.

Liberalism revived in the 1970s. Oil shocks, multinational firms and the spread of trade made states depend on each other. Robert Keohane and Joseph Nye wrote Power and Interdependence (1977).

Complex interdependence has three features

  1. Multiple channels link societies: governments, firms, NGOs, individuals. States are not the only actors.
  2. No fixed hierarchy of issues. Security does not always come first. Trade or climate can top the agenda.
  3. Military force is less useful among interdependent states.

They also showed that interdependence is unequal. Sensitivity is how fast a change in one country hurts another. Vulnerability is how costly it is to escape. The less vulnerable party has more bargaining power.

Nye later coined soft power (Bound to Lead, 1990).

Keohane's After Hegemony: Cooperation and Discord in the World Political Economy (1984) is the key text of neoliberal institutionalism.

His puzzle: if realists say cooperation depends on a dominant power (hegemonic stability), why did cooperation continue after US dominance declined in the 1970s? His answer: international regimes.

Stephen Krasner's definition (1982-83) of regimes: sets of principles, norms, rules and decision-making procedures around which actors' expectations converge. GATT and the IMF are examples.

What institutions do

  • Cut transaction costs of making deals.
  • Share information and reduce cheating.
  • Create repeated games, so a state values its reputation. Robert Axelrod's The Evolution of Cooperation (1984) showed "tit for tat" works in repeated dealings.

Keohane accepts the realist base: anarchy, and states as rational actors. He argues only that cooperation is still possible.

Other liberal arguments focus on the type of state.

  • Democratic peace. Michael Doyle, in "Kant, Liberal Legacies, and Foreign Affairs" (1983), noted that liberal democracies almost never fight each other. Bruce Russett's Grasping the Democratic Peace (1993) tested it with data.
  • Commercial peace. Trade makes war costly. This goes back to Montesquieu, Cobden and Norman Angell's The Great Illusion (1910).
  • End of history. Francis Fukuyama's essay (1989) and book (1992) saw liberal democracy as the final form of government.

Andrew Moravcsik (1997) built a general liberal theory: state preferences come from domestic society, not just from the international structure.

Critiques

Democracies do fight non-democracies (Iraq 2003). Mansfield and Snyder (1995) found democratising states are war-prone. Trade did not stop war in 1914. Realists see only chance, or US power behind the "peace".

The 1980s-90s "neo-neo debate" (David Baldwin edited Neorealism and Neoliberalism, 1993) was narrower than the first debate. Both sides accept anarchy and rational, self-interested states.

The gap: relative versus absolute gains. Joseph Grieco (1988) argued that states ask "who gains more?" and so fear cooperation. Liberals say states ask "do I gain?"

John Mearsheimer's "The False Promise of International Institutions" (1994-95) says institutions have little independent effect. Liberals reply with evidence from trade, arms control and the EU.

cards.h: Nehru's idealism and India's liberal streak
cards.b:
India was an original member of the League of Nations (1920) and a founding member of the UN (1945). Jawaharlal Nehru brought a strong idealist tone: peaceful coexistence, Panchsheel (1954), anti-colonialism and support for disarmament.

India is among the largest contributors of troops to UN peacekeeping. It champions the Global South inside the UN and the WTO.

The liberal side shows up today in:

  • The International Solar Alliance, launched with France at the Paris climate summit in 2015.
  • India's G20 presidency in 2023. The New Delhi Declaration was adopted by consensus, and the African Union became a permanent member.
  • Its theme, "One Earth, One Family, One Future", draws on Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam.

But India is also a realist. After the 1962 war with China and the 1998 Pokhran tests, it blends the two traditions. It is wary of institutions that limit its sovereignty, such as the NPT.

"Critically examine the idealist approach to international relations."
"Explain liberal institutionalism. How does it differ from neorealism?"
"Does the democratic peace thesis hold? Discuss."
"Why did the League of Nations fail?"

Structure: start with the WWI context and Kant's roots. Then Wilson and the League, with 3 reasons for failure. Add Carr's critique. Move to the modern turn: Keohane and Nye (complex interdependence), regimes and cooperation, democratic peace. Give the neo-neo debate in a short table. Finish with India: Nehru's idealism, UN peacekeeping and the ISA, and its limits.

Show balance. Say idealism did not vanish. It returned in new form.

quiz.q: Who gave the Fourteen Points speech in January 1918?
Which work by Immanuel Kant is the foundation of the democratic peace idea?
o: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals
quiz.w: Perpetual Peace (1795) set out the republican constitution and federation of free states.

quiz.q: The League of Nations' sanctions against an aggressor were provided in:
quiz.w: Article 16 of the Covenant provided sanctions; Article 10 guarded territorial integrity.

quiz.q: Which event was the League's test in 1935?
quiz.w: Italy invaded Abyssinia (Ethiopia) in 1935. Manchuria was 1931.

quiz.q: E.H. Carr's The Twenty Years' Crisis (1939) argued that the idealists:
o: Mistook wishes for facts and hid power interests behind a 'harmony of interests'
Ignored the role of morality entirely
quiz.w: Carr called them utopians and said the harmony of interests served satisfied powers.
Robert Keohane and Joseph Nye wrote Power and Interdependence (1977).

o: Cooperation ends when a hegemon declines
Regimes sustain cooperation even after hegemony declines
quiz.w: Regimes cut costs and share information, so cooperation can outlive hegemony.

quiz.q: In the 'neo-neo' debate, Joseph Grieco stressed:
quiz.w: Grieco (1988): states worry about who gains more, which limits cooperation.

quiz.q: Which statement about the democratic peace is a critique?
o: Democratising states can be war-prone (Mansfield and Snyder)
Democratic states rarely fight each other
quiz.w: Mansfield and Snyder (1995) found transitional democracies prone to war.

quiz.q: India's G20 presidency in 2023 ended with:
o: The New Delhi Declaration adopted by consensus and the AU made a permanent member
quiz.w: The Delhi summit of 9-10 September 2023 adopted a consensus declaration and admitted the African Union.
